 1.1 Digital image, image as matrix/function, image types NUM 2024-25



 Digital image: a two-dimensional function f(x, y), where x and y are spatial (plane) coordinates and the amplitude f at (x, y) is
 the intensity or gray level. When x, y and the amplitude are all finite, discrete quantities the image is digital.


A digital image is made of a finite number of elements, each with a location and a value — called picture elements, image
elements, pels or pixels (pixel is the most common term). A digital image is stored in a computer as an M × N matrix (M rows =
vertical resolution, N columns = horizontal resolution); total pixels = M × N. Image processing = manipulating this matrix by
algorithms; the camera replaces the eye and the computer replaces the brain.


 f(x,y) = [ f(0,0) … f(0,N−1) ; … ; f(M−1,0) … f(M−1,N−1) ] , L = 2k gray levels, k =
 bits/pixel


Image types

 Type Bits / pixel Values Remarks

 Binary (bi-level, bit-mapped) 1 0 = black, 1 = white Shapes, line drawings, masks, text scans

 Gray-scale (monochrome) 8 0 (black) … 255 (white) 256 shades; no colour component

 True colour (RGB) 24 (3 × 8) R, G, B each 0…255 224 = 16,777,216 colours; three-band image


A colour image converts to gray with X = 0.30 R + 0.59 G + 0.11 B . More bits per pixel ⇒ more gray levels ⇒ better
quality but larger size.

Resolution & units
 Spatial resolution – number of pixels (rows × columns); more pixels = better detail. Gray-level (intensity) resolution – number
 of bits/levels per pixel.
 DPI (dots per inch) – scanners/printers; PPI (pixels per inch) – monitors (≈72); LPI – printer lines per inch; SPI – scanner
 samples per inch.

 Image size = M × N × k bits = M × N × k / 8 bytes (colour: × number of planes).

 1.2 Sampling, quantization & spatial / gray-level resolution
 PYQ 2022-23 2023-24 2024-25 NUM 2022-23 2024-25



 Sampling = digitising the coordinate values (x, y). Quantization = digitising the amplitude (gray-level) values. Together they
 convert a continuous image f(x, y) into a digital image.


Unit 1 — Image Fundamentals Made by Jay Naik Page 4 of 43

Sampling picks equally spaced points along a scan line; quantization assigns each sample to one of the allowed discrete gray levels.


 1. A continuous image is continuous in both coordinates and amplitude (noise appears as random variation along the line).

 2. Take equally spaced samples along each line — the set of sample locations gives the sampled function; its values are still
 continuous.
 3. Divide the gray scale into L discrete levels (e.g. 8) and assign each sample to the nearest level (vertical proximity).

 4. Repeat line by line from the top → a 2-D digital image (M × N matrix).

Effects

 Sampling (spatial resolution) Quantization (gray-level resolution)

 Controls Number of pixels M × N Number of levels L = 2k

 Too few Blocky / checkerboard effect, loss of detail, aliasing False contouring (visible bands) in smooth
 areas

 Too many Larger file, more memory/bandwidth, slower processing Larger file; little visible gain beyond ≈ 8 bits

 Sampling Sample at ≥ 2 × highest spatial frequency (Nyquist), else aliasing / —
 theorem moiré



 Note: Down-sampling (e.g. 1280×720 → 640×360) keeps every alternate row/column after low-pass filtering to avoid
 aliasing; up-sampling restores size by replication or interpolation (some detail is lost for good). Bits required to store the
 image = M × N × k.

Neighbours of a pixel p(x, y)
 N4(p) – 4-neighbours: (x±1, y), (x, y±1) (horizontal & vertical).

 ND(p) – 4 diagonal neighbours: (x±1, y±1).

 N8(p) = N4 ∪ ND – 8-neighbours.

Let V be the set of gray levels used to define adjacency (binary image: V = {1}; gray image: any subset of 0…255). Two pixels are
connected only if they are neighbours and their gray levels belong to V.


 Adjacency Condition for p, q with values in V

 4-adjacency q ∈ N4(p)

 8-adjacency q ∈ N8(p)

 m-adjacency (mixed) q ∈ N4(p), or q ∈ ND(p) and N4(p) ∩ N4(q) contains no pixel with value in V



 Why m-adjacency: m-adjacency was introduced to remove the ambiguity (multiple paths) of 8-adjacency: a diagonal link is
 allowed only when the two shared 4-neighbours are not in V.


Path, connected set, region, boundary
 Path from p to q – sequence of distinct adjacent pixels p = p0, p1, …, pn = q; n is the path length (4-, 8- or m-path).

 Connected component of S containing p – the set of pixels of S connected to p; if S has only one component it is a connected
 set.

 Region R – a subset that is a connected set. Regions Ri, Rj are adjacent if their union is a connected set; otherwise disjoint (use
 4- or 8-adjacency).
 Boundary (border) of a finite region – the set of pixels in the region having at least one neighbour outside it; it forms a closed
 path (a global concept). An edge is a local concept based on gray-level discontinuity at a point. If R is the whole image, its
 boundary = first & last rows and columns.


 4-connectivity 8-connectivity

 Uses only horizontal/vertical neighbours (4) Uses horizontal, vertical and diagonal neighbours (8)

 Fewer connections → objects may break into more components More connections → objects stay joined; gives paradoxes (object
 and background both connected)

 Background then uses 8-connectivity to stay consistent Background then uses 4-connectivity

 2.1 Image enhancement & the spatial domain PYQ 2023-24



 Image enhancement processes an image so that the result is more suitable than the original for a specific application. It is
 subjective (depends on the viewer/application) and cosmetic — it adds no new information, it only improves visual quality of
 existing data.


 Spatial domain – direct manipulation of pixels in the image plane: g(x,y) = T[f(x,y)], T acts on a pixel or its neighbourhood. Two
 categories: intensity (point) transformations (contrast manipulation, thresholding) and spatial filtering / neighbourhood
 processing (smoothing, sharpening).
 Frequency domain – modify the Fourier transform of the image, then invert.

 Spatial methods are computationally cheaper. Neighbourhood operator T moves its origin pixel-by-pixel (top-left, row by row);
 at borders either ignore outside neighbours or pad with 0 (or other value) — padding thickness depends on mask size.


 Note: Applications: medical (X-ray/CT) enhancement, remote sensing, forensic/fingerprint, photography, industrial
 inspection, satellite imagery, document restoration.

 2.5 Bit-plane slicing PYQ 2023-24 2025-26 NUM 2022-23 2023-24



 An 8-bit image is a stack of 8 one-bit planes: plane 0 = least significant bit (LSB), plane 7 = MSB. Bit-plane slicing extracts

 2.6 Non-linear: log transform & power-law (gamma)
 PYQ 2023-24 2024-25 2025-26 NUM 2022-23 2024-25 2025-26



 Log transform: s = c·log(1 + r) — maps a narrow range of low (dark) input values to a wide output range and compresses
 high values: dynamic range compression. Power-law (gamma): s = c·rγ.


 Log: expands dark pixels, compresses bright ones; used to display Fourier spectra with huge dynamic range. Inverse log does
 the opposite. c is a scaling constant.

 γ < 1 – expands dark values (image brighter, washed out as γ→0); γ > 1 – compresses dark values (image darker); γ = 1 identity.

 Gamma correction – CRTs/displays respond as r≈2.5; pre-processing the image with s = r1/2.5 cancels the distortion. Also used
 for contrast manipulation (γ<1 for washed-out dark images, γ>1 for bright washed-out ones).


 Note: Log of 0 is undefined — hence 1 + r. Both are monotonic, one-to-one mappings used with output scaling to [0, L−1].

2.7 Neighbourhood processing: smoothing (low-pass) filters
 PYQ 2022-23 2024-25 2025-26 NUM 2022-23 2023-24 2024-25 MTT 26-27



 Neighbourhood (mask) processing: slide a w×w mask over the image; multiply each mask coefficient with the corresponding
 pixel, sum, and put the result at the centre pixel. Unlike point processing it uses the pixel and its neighbours.


 Spatial filters = masks/kernels/templates/windows. Linear filters correspond one-to-one to frequency-domain filters; spatial
 filters also allow non-linear filtering (median, max, min) impossible in the frequency domain.
 Noise arises in acquisition (sensor, lighting) and transmission; it is a high-frequency signal.

Smoothing (low-pass) filters
Used for blurring (removing small details before object extraction, bridging small gaps in lines) and noise reduction. They remove
high-frequency content; side effect: edges (also sharp intensity transitions) get blurred. They also smooth false contours caused
by too few gray levels.

 Filter Mask (3×3) Property

 Averaging (box) 1/9 × all ones Equal weights; strongest blur

 Weighted 1/16 × [1 2 1; 2 4 2; 1 2 1] Centre weighted highest, weights fall with
 average distance → less blurring

 Gaussian Samples of e−(x²+y²)/2σ², normalised (3×3, σ≈0.85 gives the Isotropic, no ringing; blur grows with σ; separable
 weighted mask above)


 Mask coefficients of a smoothing filter are positive and sum to 1 (brightness unchanged).

 Larger mask / larger σ ⇒ more blurring.

 Gaussian: 2-D bell surface; centre has highest value; kernel is slid across the image, weights ∝ closeness to centre, so near
 pixels influence more than far ones.


 Note: Smoothing filters (low-pass: blur, reduce noise) vs sharpening filters (high-pass: emphasise edges/detail, but amplify
 noise). Smoothing is done before edge detection to suppress noise-induced false edges.

 2.9 Sharpening (high-pass) filters: Laplacian, unsharp & high-boost
 PYQ 2025-26 NUM 2025-26



 Sharpening highlights transitions in intensity. Averaging ≈ integration, so sharpening is done by spatial differentiation:
 derivative response ∝ degree of discontinuity, so edges and fine details (and noise) are emphasised, slowly varying areas
 suppressed.


 High-pass mask e.g. [−1 −1 −1; −1 8 −1; −1 −1 −1]: sum of coefficients = 0 → flat regions give 0; a pixel brighter than its
 neighbours is boosted. Issues: negative outputs (clip to 0 / scale) and out-of-range values at strong edges (scale the mask).
 Laplacian (isotropic 2nd derivative): ∇²f = f(x+1,y)+f(x−1,y)+f(x,y+1)+f(x,y−1) − 4f(x,y). Sharpened image g = f − ∇²f (negative
 centre mask) or g = f + ∇²f (positive-centre mask). Highlights intensity discontinuities (double response at edges).

 Unsharp masking: blur the image → subtract blurred from original to get the mask gmask = f − f̄ → add it back: g = f + gmask.

 High-boost filtering: g = f + k·gmask (k > 1) — equivalent to g = (A−1)f + high-pass; k = 1 is unsharp masking; k > 1 emphasises
 detail more.


 Note: Over-doing high-pass filtering exaggerates faint details & noise and degrades the image. Low-pass and high-pass are
 complementary: high-pass = original − low-pass.

 2.10 Histogram processing & histogram equalization
 PYQ 2022-23 NUM 2022-23 2023-24 2024-25 2025-26 MTT 26-27



 The histogram of a digital image is the discrete function h(rk) = nk (number of pixels with gray level rk); the normalised
 histogram p(rk) = nk/MN estimates the probability of occurrence of rk.


 Image Histogram appearance

 Dark Concentrated on the low (left) end

 Bright Concentrated on the high (right) end

 Low contrast Narrow, centred band (dull, washed-out gray look)

 High contrast Spread over the whole range, fairly uniform → large variety of grays



 Histogram equalization (HE) automatically spreads the gray levels using the transform sk = T(rk) = (L−1) Σj=0..k p(rj) — i.e.
 (L−1) × CDF — to obtain an image with a nearly uniform histogram (high dynamic range).


 1. Compute the histogram nk and PDF p(rk) = nk/MN.

 2. Compute the cumulative sum (CDF).

 3. Multiply the CDF by (L−1) and round to the nearest integer.
 4. Map each rk → sk; levels mapping to the same s are merged (counts added).

 Conditions on T(r): (1) monotonically increasing (no intensity reversals), (2) 0 ≤ T(r) ≤ L−1 (same output range), (3) strictly
 monotonic ⇒ one-to-one inverse.

 A histogram is only an approximation of a PDF and no new intensity levels are created, so a perfectly flat histogram is rare —
 result has fewer distinct levels.
 Global HE uses the whole image; local (adaptive) HE equalises small sub-images/neighbourhoods to enhance local detail.

 Limitation: can over-enhance noise and give unnatural look; it is automatic (no parameters).

 Transforms give a compact representation (storage/transmission, compression), simplify correlation and convolution, and

 Properties desired: orthogonality / unitarity (energy preserved, inverse = conjugate transpose), separability (2-D via 1-D row-
 column), fast algorithms, energy compaction.


 3.1 Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT)

 The Fourier transform decomposes an image into sine/cosine components of different spatial frequencies. 2-D DFT: F(u,v) =
 ΣxΣy f(x,y) e−j2π(ux/M + vy/N); inverse: f(x,y) = (1/MN) ΣΣ F(u,v) e+j2π(ux/M + vy/N).


 Why Fourier: noise removal (drop high frequencies), edge detection (emphasise high frequencies), compression (find low-
 energy regions); spatial filtering (multiply-add per pixel) becomes a simple multiplication in the frequency domain.

 Spectrum |F(u,v)|; DC term F(0,0) = sum of all pixels (average brightness × MN). After centring (multiplying by (−1)x+y) low
 frequencies are at the centre. Log scaling is used to display it.
 Properties: separability, linearity, translation (shift in space = phase change), periodicity (period N), conjugate symmetry for
 real images, rotation, scaling, convolution theorem f*h ⇔ F·H, Parseval (energy conservation), average value = F(0,0)/MN.

 FFT reduces complexity from O(N²) to O(N log N).

 5.5 Canny edge detector

 Canny is the optimal step-edge detector with three goals: (1) low error rate — find all true edges, no spurious ones; (2) good

 Video signal = a sequence of time-varying images called frames; a real scene is a 3-D signal f(x, y, z, t). An illusion of

 8.5 Three-Step Search (TSS) & New Three-Step Search (NTSS) PYQ 2022-23 2024-25 2025-26



 TSS is a fast, coarse-to-fine search that evaluates only 25 locations for p = 7 instead of 225 (a 9× reduction).


 1. Start at the centre (0,0) of the search window; step size S = (p+1)/2 = 4.
 2. Evaluate the SAD of 9 points: the centre and 8 points at ±S around it (a 3×3 grid with spacing S).

 3. Move the centre to the point with minimum SAD; halve the step: S = S/2.
 4. Repeat (8 new points per step) until S = 1; the best point at S = 1 gives the motion vector. Total = 9 + 8 + 8 = 25.

Encoder: current frame − motion-compensated prediction (from frame memory + motion estimation) → prediction error

so it can regenerate the prediction itself.
